title: Infantino Under Siege: UEFA and Concacaf Demand Leadership Review at FIFA
summary: Gianni Infantino's hold on FIFA is looking shakier than ever. On Saturday, both UEFA and Concacaf—the governing bodies for European and North/Central American soccer—publicly rebuked the FIFA president, demanding a 'full review' of his leadership. The backlash stems from Infantino's now-scrapped proposal to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors. While UEFA welcomed the withdrawal as a 'victory for the whole game,' it didn't hold back, accusing Infantino of failing to deliver on transparency promises made during his 2016 campaign. Concacaf went further, calling the plan an 'egregious act of poor governance' and a 'symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first.' The statements mark an unprecedented public rift between FIFA and its most powerful confederations. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has already called for Infantino to resign. Only Qatar's football association has voiced support, praising Infantino's 'wisdom' in prioritizing unity. The timing is critical: Infantino seeks a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in March. With trust eroded, his path to re-election now looks uncertain. As Concacaf bluntly stated, 'Accountability cannot be optional.'
why_it_matters: The leadership crisis at FIFA affects the future of the world’s most popular sport, including decisions about tournaments worth billions of dollars. For young fans, it shows how power struggles in sports organizations can influence everything from ticket prices to where the next World Cup is played.

background_read: Gianni Infantino became FIFA president in 2016 after a huge corruption scandal forced his predecessor out; he promised to make the organization more transparent and ethical.

UEFA, based in Switzerland, represents 55 European soccer nations and runs the Champions League; Concacaf oversees soccer in North America, Central America, and the Caribbean, including the U.S. and Mexico.
FIFA's Congress is the gathering of all 211 member national soccer associations, where the president is elected; a candidate needs a majority vote to win.

Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup and other tournaments to private investors reminded many of the business-first culture that sparked earlier scandals, even though he later withdrew it under pressure.

The public split between FIFA and its most powerful confederations is rare and echoes past power struggles over money and control before the 2026 World Cup, which will be hosted by the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Infantino's grip on FIFA weakens after public rebuke from two major confederations.
KEY EVENT: UEFA and Concacaf demand full review of leadership after skaky proposal scrapped.
├─ UEFA: Called withdrawal a 'victory for the whole game,' but slammed broken transparency promises.
└─ Concacaf: Blasted plan as 'egregious act of poor governance,' symptom of leadership that stopped putting football first.

TIMING: Critical – Infantino seeks fourth term at FIFA Congress in March.
OPEN QUESTION: With trust eroded, can he still win re-election?

perspectives.description: The public call for review is seen as a long-overdue step toward restoring FIFA's credibility. If reform succeeds, soccer could be run more fairly, with money going back into the game at the grassroots level rather than private pockets.

Open infighting between FIFA and its confederations may scare off sponsors and host nations, especially ahead of the 2026 World Cup. A weak president could delay decisions, and the image of chaos might damage the sport’s global appeal.

Tensions between FIFA’s global leadership and powerful regional bodies are nothing new; they often stem from struggles over broadcasting rights, tournament slots, and revenue sharing. This episode mirrors past clashes that reshaped soccer governance after the 2015 scandal.

If Infantino loses the March election, a new president could push through stricter transparency rules and perhaps undo some of his controversial moves. But if he wins again, the confederations might keep challenging him, leading to a drawn-out power struggle that sidelines the real needs of players and fans.
